disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation) is characterized by persistent patterns of inattention, such as difficulty sustaining focus, following through on tasks, organizing activities, and remembering everyday responsibilities, without prominent hyperactive or impulsive behavior. Symptoms must be present for at least several months, cause clear functional impairment across settings (e.g., work, home, school), and typically begin in childhood even if they are not recognized until adulthood. Adults often present with chronic work underperformance, disorganization, or academic difficulties rather than overt behavioral problems, and they may come to attention during periods of increased role demands. It is distinguished from mood, anxiety, or learning disorders by the pervasiveness and early onset of attentional and organizational difficulties, though these conditions frequently co-occur.

narrative.stressor: In the past school year, Yoan took on additional responsibilities at his Worcester secondary school, including leading a new humanities curriculum overhaul and co-chairing a diversity and inclusion committee, on top of his regular teaching load. The increased number of parallel projects, planning meetings, and grading deadlines made his long-standing tendency to mismanage time and lose track of school-related obligations much more visible to colleagues and administrators. Over about 11 months, missed internal deadlines for curriculum drafts and repeated last-minute scrambles to prepare materials began affecting his reputation at work and creating tension at home as he spent evenings trying to catch up instead of being present with his wife. After a mid-year performance review highlighting concerns about reliability and documentation, and noticing that his difficulty keeping track of tasks seemed out of proportion to his effort and motivation, Yoan agreed to seek a psychiatric evaluation at the urging of his department head and his wife.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I keep starting school projects and committee work with good intentions but I can’t seem to follow through and finish things on time, no matter how hard I try to stay on top of it.”

narrative.stressor: Following her divorce about a year ago, Amanda moved into a smaller house and took on sole responsibility for her own household management while also stepping into a lead maintenance role at a larger facility. The combination of a new home to set up, more complex work orders to coordinate, and managing her finances alone created a level of logistical demand she had not previously faced. Over the last 11 months, she noticed that despite her technical competence and usual preference for order, she was increasingly missing personal appointments, overlooking bill due dates, and double-booking herself for jobs, which she initially attributed to the stress of the life change. When late fees, a near utility shutoff, and a mix-up that left a critical work repair undone on the scheduled day all occurred within a short span, Amanda became worried that something beyond normal adjustment was affecting her day-to-day functioning and sought a psychiatric assessment at the suggestion of a coworker who had been evaluated for adult ADHD.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Ever since the divorce and moving into my own place, I keep forgetting basic things like paying bills and showing up for appointments, even when I write them down.”

narrative.stressor: As Luis transitioned further into retirement and expanded his home-based catering work and church festival organizing, he found himself juggling more small but important responsibilities without the external structure of a formal job. Over the past 11 months, his wife and adult children increasingly pointed out how often he misplaced invoices, recipe notes, and church paperwork, leading to repeated trips to buy items he already had and occasional embarrassment when he showed up unprepared for community events. At first he laughed it off as getting older, but the pattern persisted even when he felt otherwise healthy and well-rested, and it began to strain his confidence in taking on new community projects. After a particularly frustrating incident where missing ingredients and lost order details disrupted a catering event for a parish family, his daughter expressed concern that his forgetfulness and disorganization seemed long-standing but were now interfering with things he cared deeply about, prompting him to agree to a psychiatric evaluation to see if there was an underlying attention problem.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Lately I keep losing important things for my catering and church work—papers, lists, even ingredients—and it’s starting to mess up events I’m responsible for.”
